quarterly_data.signal: CFO Bill George: Q3 2026 revenue was $3.8 billion, an increase of $1.3 billion or 54%; electrical segment revenue grew 85% and mechanical revenue grew 43%; through nine months same-store revenue increased 47%. Gross profit was $934 million, operating income rose 65% to $625 million (operating margin 16.6% vs 15.5%), net income was $489 million or $13.91 per share (vs $8.25), and EBITDA increased 61% to $668 million, with trailing 12-month EBITDA of approximately $2.3 billion. CEO Brian Lane: construction drives most of the results, but service revenue and profit also grew by double-digit percentages (President Trent McKenna: service revenue up 13%).
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 revenue $3.8 billion (+54%); electrical +85%, mechanical +43%; nine-month same-store +47%; EPS $13.91; EBITDA $668 million (+61%); trailing 12-month EBITDA approximately $2.3 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance (CFO Bill George): full-year 2026 same-store revenue is expected in the mid 40% range, and same-store full-year 2027 revenue is estimated to grow in the mid 20% range; 2027 gross profit margins are 'likely to continue in the strong ranges that we've achieved on average over recent quarters' (he added 'we do not represent that margins will go up in the future'); tax rate around 23% for the rest of 2026 and in 2027; full-year CapEx 4%-5% of revenue, likely to stay elevated during the first half of 2027. CEO Brian Lane: 'we expect continuing growth and strong results for the remainder of 2026 and 2027.'
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 same-store revenue growth mid 40% range; 2027 same-store revenue growth mid 20% range; CapEx 4%-5% of revenue; tax rate around 23%

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog reached a record $17.8 billion, up $8.4 billion or 90% year over year and $3.8 billion or 27% sequentially - the eighth consecutive sequential backlog increase. President Trent McKenna: Q3 bookings were especially strong in the technology sector, in both the traditional construction business and modular. CEO Brian Lane: because the company is winning larger projects, backlog duration has extended to roughly 18-24 months, which he thinks is 'a good framework' (versus nine months 10 years ago). CFO Bill George: backlog is 'really lumpy' and he does not think there is any different trend between mechanical and electrical; if more is booked in one quarter, less might be booked in a future quarter, but at this moment conditions are 'extremely supportive with no sign of that changing.'
quarterly_data.figure: backlog $17.8 billion (+$8.4 billion or 90% YoY; +$3.8 billion or 27% QoQ); duration roughly 18-24 months

quarterly_data.signal: Revenue mix (President Trent McKenna): industrial customers were 76% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 and are major drivers of pipeline and backlog; technology, included in industrial, was 59% of revenue, up from 42% in the prior year; institutional (education, healthcare, government) 16%; commercial about 8%. Construction was 90% of revenue (new buildings 75%, existing buildings 15%), modular (counted in new building construction) was 17% of revenue year to date, and service was 10%, with service profitability 'stronger than ever'.
quarterly_data.figure: technology 59% of revenue (vs 42%); industrial 76%; institutional 16%; commercial about 8%; modular 17%; service 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Modular capacity (President Trent McKenna): on track for over 4 million square feet of modular space by the end of 2026 and, with ongoing orders and investments, approximately 6 million square feet of capacity by the end of 2027; the build-out to 6 million is based on current programmatic build-outs with existing modular customers, and further investments are being evaluated. CFO Bill George: in addition to the modular expansions, Comfort invested over $100 million in CapEx to expand pre-fabrication facilities for the traditional construction business; modular plants are '250,000, 600,000, 700,000 sq ft buildings' with robots, automated paint booths and turntables, 'not scalable the way you can just print another copy of software.'
quarterly_data.figure: over 4 million square feet by end of 2026; approximately 6 million square feet by end of 2027; over $100 million CapEx for pre-fabrication facilities

quarterly_data.signal: Modular customers: the company is building modular products for new customers, including a frontier lab and colocation providers ('That's real work'), but has not yet entered arrangements it would call programmatic (President Trent McKenna). CFO Bill George: programmatic customers have typically made five-year volume commitments before Comfort spends large CapEx on space for their product; Comfort has tended to stick with its two big customers (one for 20 years), who 'want more than we can buy' and are looking at other sources of supply; for a newer customer to graduate to programmatic, the two things he would look for are the nature of the commitment and the payment timing, and Comfort's long experience 'really, really takes into account the financial strength of our counterparties'. Modular receives mobilization payments and payments upon delivery and is 'vastly ahead' with programmatic customers; outside modular the payment obligation typically comes from a large national general contractor. Many of the newer customers are new to building modular hot aisle containment or modular chiller plants.
quarterly_data.figure: five-year volume commitments; two big customers

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity is the limit, not demand. President Trent McKenna: 'the governor isn't demand, the governor's really just labor'; customers are committing earlier and for larger scopes 'because they know that capacity like ours is scarce right now' and want to lock up Comfort's capacity; new customers are creeping in; demand 'remains well in excess of what the industry can actually deliver'; every dollar in backlog is labor-planned, and headcount (over 25,000 today) will have to grow for mid-20s growth in 2027; the traveling workforce, the contract craft operations at Kodiak and Pivot and acquisitions like Hunt and Boys have helped. CFO Bill George: 'Let's say we have 40 businesses, 20 are highly exposed to the super cycle. Those people have more work than they can do.'. CEO Brian Lane: confident the current backlog can be executed with the existing forces.

Margins (CFO Bill George): gross margin held at 24.8%; mechanical segment gross margin rose to 25.1% from 24.3%, while electrical slipped to 24.3% from 26.2% (last year's Q3 included discrete gains, including a customer emerging from bankruptcy, worth approximately 1.8%; without them electrical margins were roughly flat). Sequential margin pressure came from material and equipment running about 2% higher in the cost mix than the first-half average (early-stage large jobs, long pipe runs), purchase-accounting adjustments about $12 million higher than in Q2, and one large electrical company (over half of the segment) whose gross margin was in the 30s in Q2 and in Q3 was still 'unfathomably high' and above the company average but not in the 30s; with the company early in a lot of jobs, he thinks 'we'll get back to average first half of next year' and says gross profit per hour worked continues to improve. Modular has closed the gap to parity with average margins and is the single largest driver of higher mechanical operating margins. SG&A was $314 million, 8.3% of revenue (vs $230 million, 9.4%).
quarterly_data.figure: gross margin 24.8%; mechanical 25.1% (vs 24.3%); electrical 24.3% (vs 26.2%); purchase adjustments about $12 million higher; SG&A $314 million (8.3%)

quarterly_data.signal: Cash flow (CFO Bill George): Q3 free cash flow was $806 million and year-to-date cash flow roughly $2 billion, helped by advantageous payment terms and favorable collections from large technology customers and by $166 million of income tax payments deferred until the fourth quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 free cash flow $806 million; year-to-date roughly $2 billion; $166 million tax payments deferred

quarterly_data.signal: Acquisitions (CEO Brian Lane): on August 1st Comfort acquired Boys Electrical (Melbourne, Florida) and NeoPod, a modular company for the healthcare industry based in New Braunfels, Texas; together they are expected to contribute over $100 million in annual revenue at good margins. CFO Bill George: the acquisition pipeline is very good, though pricing for acquisitions has been high and he thinks it 'might be rolling over right now'.

Data-center risks: CEO Brian Lane said that for the prospects Comfort is looking at, the power connection is usually already solved because it is a late-cycle player in a building's design, and that for the work Comfort has today, 'we have not been delayed by any moratorium'; CFO Bill George said power 'really hasn't delayed anything we're seeing', that many data centers generate their own power, and that political moratorium rhetoric has not changed any project's trajectory he knows of but he has a sense it may push more of the work into more friendly jurisdictions; President Trent McKenna noted modular is even less exposed because it ships to wherever the customer site is.

Geography (CEO Brian Lane, CFO Bill George): Texas is really strong, Georgia strong and getting stronger, Louisiana strong, Utah very strong, plus North and South Carolina and the Southeast, and Iowa has woken up ('Iowa's woken up') with a new factory. In Arizona the next phases of big semiconductor work are about to hit ('monster work'); the CFO said Comfort has opportunities there but may not take much because it is so busy in Texas.
